entries.3f88d4dce613947ae1589a3f51fe329adbb5788b: <div sID="gen5424" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="1Sam.10" sID="1Sam.10"/> <div eID="gen5424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5425" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5426" type="x-p"/> We left Samuel and Saul walking together, probably some private way over the fields down from Ramah, perhaps in the paths of the vineyards, and Saul expecting to hear from Samuel the word of God. Now here we have, I. The anointing of Saul then and there, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.1">ver. 1</reference>. The signs Samuel gave him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.2-1Sam.10.6">ver. 2-6</reference>. And instructions, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.7-1Sam.10.8">ver. 7-8</reference>. II. The accomplishment of those signs to the satisfaction of Saul, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.9-1Sam.10.13">ver. 9-13</reference>. III. His return to his father's house, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.14-1Sam.10.16">ver. 14-16</reference>. IV. His public election by lot, and solemn inauguration, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.17-1Sam.10.25">ver. 17-25</reference>. V. His return to his own city, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.26-1Sam.10.27">ver. 26, 27</reference>. It is a great work that is here a doing, the setting up not only of a monarch, but of monarchy itself, in Israel; and therefore in all the advances towards it much of God is seen.
entries.a8dd291ac932c751e6cd8d354d5e9f210a1766da: <div eID="gen5426" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5425" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Saul Anointed by Samuel; Samuel's Address to Saul. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1070.)</title> <div sID="gen5427" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then Samuel took a vial of oil, and poured <hi type="italic">it</hi> upon his head, and kissed him, and said, <hi type="italic">Is it</hi> not because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath anointed thee <hi type="italic">to be</hi> captain over his inheritance? <hi type="super">2</hi> When thou art departed from me to day, then thou shalt find two men by Rachel's sepulchre in the border of Benjamin at Zelzah; and they will say unto thee, The asses which thou wentest to seek are found: and, lo, thy father hath left the care of the asses, and sorroweth for you, saying, What shall I do for my son? <hi type="super">3</hi> Then shalt thou go on forward from thence, and thou shalt come to the plain of Tabor, and there shall meet thee three men going up to God to Bethel, one carrying three kids, and another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a bottle of wine: <hi type="super">4</hi> And they will salute thee, and give thee two <hi type="italic">loaves</hi> of bread; which thou shalt receive of their hands. <hi type="super">5</hi> After that thou shalt come to the hill of God, where <hi type="italic">is</hi> the garrison of the Philistines: and it shall come to pass, when thou art come thither to the city, that thou shalt meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place with a psaltery, and a tabret, and a pipe, and a harp, before them; and they shall prophesy: <hi type="super">6</hi> And the Spirit of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will come upon thee, and thou shalt prophesy with them, and shalt be turned into another man. <hi type="super">7</hi> And let it be, when these signs are come unto thee, <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou do as occasion serve thee; for God <hi type="italic">is</hi> with thee. <hi type="super">8</hi> And thou shalt go down before me to Gilgal; and, behold, I will come down unto thee, to offer burnt offerings, <hi type="italic">and</hi> to sacrifice sacrifices of peace offerings: seven days shalt thou tarry, till I come to thee, and shew thee what thou shalt do. <div eID="gen5427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5428" type="x-p"/> Samuel is here executing the office of a prophet, giving Saul full assurance from God that he should be king, as he was afterwards, according to these prophecies which went before of him. <div eID="gen5428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5429" type="x-p"/> I. He <hi type="italic">anointed him</hi> and <hi type="italic">kissed him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.1">v. 1</reference>. This was not done in a solemn assembly, but it was done by divine appointment, which made up the want of all external solemnities, nor was it ever the less valid for its being done in private, under a hedge, or, as the Jews say, by <hi type="italic">a fountain.</hi> God's institutions are great and honourable, though the circumstances of their administration be ever so mean and despicable. 1. Samuel, by anointing Saul, assured him that it was God's act to make him king: <hi type="italic">Is it not because the Lord hath anointed thee?</hi> And, in token of that, the high priest was anointed to his office, to signify the conferring of those gifts upon him that were requisite for the discharge of its duties, and the same was intimated in the anointing of kings; for whom God calls he qualifies, and suitable qualifications furnish good proof of a commission. These sacred unctions, then used, pointed at the great Messiah, or anointed one, the king of the church, and high priest of our profession, who was anointed with the oil of the Spirit, not by measure, but without measure, and above all the priests and princes of the Jewish church. It was common oil, no doubt, which Samuel used, and we read not of his blessing it or praying over it. But it was only a vial of oil that he anointed him with, the vessel brittle, because his kingdom would soon be cracked and broken, and the quantity small, because he had but little of the Spirit conferred upon him to what David had, who was therefore anointed with a horn of oil, as were Solomon and Jehu with a box of oil. 2. By kissing him, he assured him of his own approbation of the choice, not only his consent to it, but his complacency in it, though it abridged his power and eclipsed his glory and the glory of his family. "<hi type="italic">God has anointed thee,</hi>" says Samuel, "<hi type="italic">to be king,</hi> and I am satisfied and very well pleased, in pledge of which take this kiss." It was likewise a kiss of homage and allegiance; hereby he not only owns him to be king, but his king, and in this sense we are commanded to <hi type="italic">kiss the Son,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.12">Ps. ii. 12</reference>. God has anointed him, and therefore we must thus acknowledge him and do homage to him. In Samuel's explication of the ceremony, he reminds him, (1.) Of the nature of the government to which he is called. He was anointed to be a captain, a commander indeed, which bespeaks honour and power, but a commander in war, which bespeaks care, and toil, and danger. (2.) Of the origin of it: <hi type="italic">The Lord hath anointed thee.</hi> By him he ruled, and therefore must rule for him, in dependence on him, and with an eye to his glory. (3.) Of the end of it. It is over his inheritance, to take care of that, protect it, and order all the affairs of it for the best, as a steward whom a great man sets over his estate, to manage it for his service and give an account of it to him. <div eID="gen5429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5430" type="x-p"/> II. For his further satisfaction he gives him some signs, which should come to pass immediately, this very day; and they were such as would not only confirm the word of Samuel in general, and prove him a true prophet, but would confirm this word to Saul in particular, that he should be king. 1. He should presently meet with some that would bring him intelligence from home of the care his father's house was in concerning him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.2">v. 2</reference>. These he would meet hard by Rachel's sepulchre. The first place Samuel directed him to was a sepulchre, the sepulchre of one of his ancestors, for Rachel died in travail with Benjamin; there he must read a lecture of his own mortality, and now that he had a crown in his eye must think of his grave, in which all his honour would be laid in the dust. Here two men would meet him, perhaps sent on purpose to look after him, and would tell him the asses were found, and his father was in pain concerning him, saying, <hi type="italic">What shall I do for my son?</hi> He would reckon it happened well that he met with these messengers; and it is good to eye Providence in favourable conjunctures (though the matter be minute) and to be encouraged to trust it in greater matters. 2. He should next meet with others going to Bethel, where, it should seem, there was a high place for religious worship, and these men were bringing their sacrifices thither, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.3-1Sam.10.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. It was a token for good to one that was designed for the government of Israel, wherever he came, to meet with people going to worship God. It is supposed that those kids and loaves, and the bottle of wine which the three men had with them, were designed for sacrifice, with the meat-offerings and drink-offerings that were to attend the sacrifice; yet Samuel tells Saul that they will give him two of their loaves, and he must take them. Such a present would look to us now like the relieving of a beggar. Saul must hereafter remember the time when he received alms, and must therefore be humble and charitable to the poor. But perhaps it would then be construed a fit present for a prince; and, as such, Saul must receive it, the first present that was brought to him, by such as knew not what they did, nor why they did it, but God put it into their hearts, which made it the more fit to be a sign to him. These two loaves, which were the first tribute paid to this newly-anointed king, might serve for an admonition to him not to spend the wealth of his crown in luxury, but still to be content with plain food. Bread is the staff of life. 3. The most remarkable sign of all would be his joining with a company of prophets that he should meet with, under the influence of a spirit of prophecy, which should at that time come upon him. What God works in us by his Spirit serves much more for the confirming of faith than any thing wrought for us by his providence. He here (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.5-1Sam.10.6">v. 5, 6</reference>) tells him, (1.) Where this would happen: <hi type="italic">At the hill of God,</hi> where there was a <hi type="italic">garrison of the Philistines,</hi> which is supposed to be near Gibeah, his own city, for there was the Philistines' garrison, <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.3">ch. xiii. 3</reference>. Perhaps it was one of the articles of Samuel's agreement with them that they should have a garrison there, or, rather, after they were subdued in the beginning of his time they got ground again, so far as to force this garrison into that place, and thence God raised up the man that should chastise them. There was a place that was called the <hi type="italic">hill of God,</hi> because of one of the schools of the prophets built upon it; and such respect did even Philistines themselves pay to religion that a garrison of their soldiers suffered a school of God's prophets to live peaceably by them, and did not only not dislodge them, but not restrain nor disturb the public exercises of their devotion. (2.) Upon what occasion; he should meet <hi type="italic">a company of prophets with music before them, prophesying,</hi> and with them he should join himself. These prophets were not (as it should seem) divinely inspired to foretel things to come, nor did God reveal himself to them by dreams and visions, but they employed themselves in the study of the law, in instructing their neighbours, and in the acts of piety, especially in praising God, wherein they were wonderfully assisted and enlarged by the Spirit of God. It was happy for Israel that they had not only prophets, but companies of prophets, who gave them good instructions and set them good examples, and helped very much to keep up religion among them. Now the word of the Lord was not precious, as it had been when Samuel was first raised up, who had been instrumental in founding these colleges, or religious houses, whence, it is probable, the synagogues took their rise. What a pity was it that Israel should be weary of the government of such a man, who though he had not, as a man of war, expelled the Philistines, yet (which was a greater kindness to Israel) had, as a man of God, settled the schools of the prophets! Music was then used as a proper means to dispose the mind to receive the impressions of the good Spirit, as it did Elisha's, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.15">2 Kings iii. 15</reference>. But we have no reason to look for the same benefit by it now, unless we saw it as effectual as it was then in Saul's case, to drive away the evil spirit. These prophets had been at the high place, probably offering sacrifice, and now they came back singing psalms. We should come from holy ordinances with our hearts greatly enlarged in holy joy and praise. See <reference osisRef="Ps.138.5">Ps. cxxxviii. 5</reference>. Saul should find himself strongly moved to join with them, and should be turned thereby <hi type="italic">into another man</hi> from what he had been while he lived in a private capacity. The Spirit of God, by his ordinances, changes men, wonderfully transforms them; Saul, by praising God in the communion of saints, became another man, but whether a new man or no may be questioned. <div eID="gen5430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5431" type="x-p"/> III. He directs him to proceed in the administration of his government as Providence should lead him, and as Samuel should advise him. 1. He must follow Providence in ordinary cases (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Do as occasion shall serve thee.</hi> Take such measures as thy own prudence shall direct thee." But, 2. In an extraordinary strait that would hereafter befal him at Gilgal, and would be the most critical juncture of all, when he would have special need of divine aids, he must wait for Samuel to come to him, and must tarry <hi type="italic">seven days</hi> in expectation of him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.8">v. 8</reference>. How his failing in this matter proved his fall we find afterwards, <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.11">ch. xiii. 11</reference>. It was now a plain intimation to him that he was upon his good behaviour, and, though a king, must act under the direction of Samuel, and do as he should order him. The greatest of men must own themselves in subjection to God and his word.
entries.049f2f4b67a5f66eceab7db1053f7c9c3b5f608f: <div eID="gen5431" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Saul Among the Prophets. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1070.)</title> <div sID="gen5432" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> And it was <hi type="italic">so,</hi> that when he had turned his back to go from Samuel, God gave him another heart: and all those signs came to pass that day. <hi type="super">10</hi> And when they came thither to the hill, behold, a company of prophets met him; and the Spirit of God came upon him, and he prophesied among them. <hi type="super">11</hi> And it came to pass, when all that knew him beforetime saw that, behold, he prophesied among the prophets, then the people said one to another, What <hi type="italic">is</hi> this <hi type="italic">that</hi> is come unto the son of Kish? <hi type="italic">Is</hi> Saul also among the prophets? <hi type="super">12</hi> And one of the same place answered and said, But who <hi type="italic">is</hi> their father? Therefore it became a proverb, <hi type="italic">Is</hi> Saul also among the prophets? <hi type="super">13</hi> And when he had made an end of prophesying, he came to the high place. <hi type="super">14</hi> And Saul's uncle said unto him and to his servant, Whither went ye? And he said, To seek the asses: and when we saw that <hi type="italic">they were</hi> no where, we came to Samuel. <hi type="super">15</hi> And Saul's uncle said, Tell me, I pray thee, what Samuel said unto you. <hi type="super">16</hi> And Saul said unto his uncle, He told us plainly that the asses were found. But of the matter of the kingdom, whereof Samuel spake, he told him not. <div eID="gen5432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5433" type="x-p"/> Saul has now taken his leave of Samuel, much amazed, we may well suppose, at what has been done to him, almost ready to question whether he be awake or no, and whether it be not all a dream. Now here we are told, <div eID="gen5433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5434" type="x-p"/> I. What occurred by the way, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.9">v. 9</reference>. Those signs which Samuel had given him came to pass very punctually; but that which gave him the greatest satisfaction of all was this, he found immediately that God had given him <hi type="italic">another heart.</hi> A new fire was kindled in his breast, such as he had never before been acquainted with: seeking the asses is quite out of his mind, and he thinks of nothing but fighting the Philistines, redressing the grievances of Israel, making laws, administering justice, and providing for the public safety; these are the things that now fill his head. He finds himself raised to such a pitch of boldness and bravery as he never thought he should be conscious of. He has no longer the heart of a husbandman, which is low, and mean, and narrow, and concerned only about his corn and cattle; but the heart of a statesman, a general, a prince. Whom God calls to any service he will make fit for it. If he advance to another station, he will give another heart, to those who sincerely desire to serve him with their power. <div eID="gen5434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5435" type="x-p"/> II. What occurred when he came near home. They came to <hi type="italic">the hill</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.10">v. 10</reference>), that is, to <hi type="italic">Gibeah,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Geba,</hi> which signifies <hi type="italic">a hill,</hi> and so the Chaldee here takes it as a proper name; he met with the prophets as Samuel had told him, and the Spirit of God came upon him, strongly and suddenly (so the word signifies), but not so as to rest and abide upon him. It came on so as to go off quickly. However, for the present, it had a strange effect upon him; for he immediately joined with the prophets in their devotion, and that with as much decorum and as great a transport of affection as any of them: <hi type="italic">He prophesied among them.</hi> Now, <div eID="gen5435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5436" type="x-p"/> 1. His prophesying was publicly taken notice of, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.11-1Sam.10.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. He was now among his acquaintance, who, when they saw him among the prophets, called one another to come and see a strange sight. This would prepare them to accept him as a king, though one of themselves, when they had seen how God had advanced him to the honour of a prophet. The seventy elders prophesied before they were made judges, <reference osisRef="Num.11.25">Num. xi. 25</reference>. Now, (1.) They all wondered to see Saul among the prophets: <hi type="italic">What is this that has come to the son of Kish?</hi> Though this school of the prophets was near his father's house, yet he had never associated with them, nor shown them any respect, perhaps had sometimes spoken slightly of them; and now to see him prophesying among them was a surprise to them, as it was long after when his namesake, in the New Testament, preached that gospel which he had before persecuted, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.21">Acts ix. 21</reference>. Where God gives another heart it will soon show itself. (2.) One of them, that was wiser than the rest, asked, "<hi type="italic">Who is their father,</hi> or instructor? Is is not God? Are they not all taught of him? Do they not all owe their gifts to him? And is he limited? Cannot he make Saul a prophet, as well as any of them, if he please?" Or, "Is not Samuel their father?" Under God, he was so; and Saul had now lately been with him, which, by his servant, he might know. No marvel for him to prophesy who lay last night under Samuel's roof. (3.) It became a proverb, commonly used in Israel, when they would express their wonder at a bad man's either becoming good, or at least being found in good company, <hi type="italic">Is Saul among the prophets?</hi> Note, Saul among the prophets is a wonder to a proverb. Let not the worst be despaired of, yet let not an external show of devotion, and a sudden change for the present, be too much relied on; for Saul among the prophets was Saul still. <div eID="gen5436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5437" type="x-p"/> 2. His being anointed was kept private. When he had done prophesying, (1.) It should seem he uttered all his words before the Lord, and recommended the affair to his favour, for he went straight <hi type="italic">to the high place</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.13">v. 13</reference>), to give God thanks for his mercies to him and to pray for the continuance of those mercies. But, (2.) He industriously concealed from his relations what had passed. His uncle, who met with him either at the high place or as soon as he came home, examined him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.14">v. 14</reference>. Saul owned, for his servant knew it, that they had been with Samuel, and that he told them the asses were found, but said not a word of <hi type="italic">the kingdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.14-1Sam.10.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. This was an instance, [1.] Of his humility. Many a one would have been so elated with this surprising elevation as to proclaim it upon the house-top. But Saul, though he might please himself with it in his own breast, did not pride himself in it among his neighbours. The heirs of the kingdom of glory are well enough pleased that <hi type="italic">the world knows them not,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.3.1">1 John iii. 1</reference>. [2.] Of his prudence. Had he been forward to proclaim it, he would have been envied, and he knew not what difficulty that might have created him. Samuel had communicated it to him as a secret, and he knows how to keep counsel. Thus it appears that he had another heart, a heart fit for government. [3.] Of his dependence upon God. He does not go about to make an interest for himself, but leaves it to God to carry on his own work by Samuel, and, for his own part, sits still, to see how the matter will fall.
entries.48ee14b199310d664b12cdc9c8348316122a15bb: <div eID="gen5437" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Election of a King; Saul Introduced to the People. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1070.)</title> <div sID="gen5438" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> And Samuel called the people together unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to Mizpeh; <hi type="super">18</hi> And said unto the children of Israel, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, I brought up Israel out of Egypt, and delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians, and out of the hand of all kingdoms, <hi type="italic">and</hi> of them that oppressed you: <hi type="super">19</hi> And ye have this day rejected your God, who himself saved you out of all your adversities and your tribulations; and ye have said unto him, <hi type="italic">Nay,</hi> but set a king over us. Now therefore present yourselves before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> by your tribes, and by your thousands. <hi type="super">20</hi> And when Samuel had caused all the tribes of Israel to come near, the tribe of Benjamin was taken. <hi type="super">21</hi> When he had caused the tribe of Benjamin to come near by their families, the family of Matri was taken, and Saul the son of Kish was taken: and when they sought him, he could not be found. <hi type="super">22</hi> Therefore they enquired of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> further, if the man should yet come thither. And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> answered, Behold, he hath hid himself among the stuff. <hi type="super">23</hi> And they ran and fetched him thence: and when he stood among the people, he was higher than any of the people from his shoulders and upward. <hi type="super">24</hi> And Samuel said to all the people, See ye him whom the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath chosen, that <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none like him among all the people? And all the people shouted, and said, God save the king. <hi type="super">25</hi> Then Samuel told the people the manner of the kingdom, and wrote <hi type="italic">it</hi> in a book, and laid <hi type="italic">it</hi> up before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . And Samuel sent all the people away, every man to his house. <hi type="super">26</hi> And Saul also went home to Gibeah; and there went with him a band of men, whose hearts God had touched. <hi type="super">27</hi> But the children of Belial said, How shall this man save us? And they despised him, and brought him no presents. But he held his peace. <div eID="gen5438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5439" type="x-p"/> Saul's nomination to the throne is here made public, in a general assembly of the elders of Israel, the representatives of their respective tribes at Mizpeh. It is probable that this convention of the states was called as soon as conveniently it might, after Saul was anointed, for, if there must be a change in their government, the sooner the better: it might be of bad consequence to be long in the doing. The people having met in a solemn assembly, in which God was in a peculiar manner present (and therefore it is said they were <hi type="italic">called together unto the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.17">v. 17</reference>), Samuel acts for God among them. <div eID="gen5439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5440" type="x-p"/> I. He reproves them for casting off the government of a prophet, and desiring that of a captain. 1. He shows them (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.18">v. 18</reference>) how happy they had been under the divine government; when God ruled them, he <hi type="italic">delivered them out of the hand of those that oppressed them,</hi> and what would they desire more? Could the mightiest man of valour do that for them which the Almighty God had done? 2. He likewise shows them (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.19">v. 19</reference>) what an affront they had put upon God (who had himself saved them <hi type="italic">out of all their tribulations,</hi> by his own power, and by such as he had immediately called and qualified) in desiring a king to save them. He tells them in plain terms, "<hi type="italic">You have this day rejected your God;</hi> you have in effect done it: so he construes it, and he might justly, for your so doing, reject you." Those that can live better by sense than by faith, that stay themselves upon an arm of flesh rather than upon the almighty arm, forsake a fountain of living waters for broken cisterns. And some make their obstinacy in this matter to be a presage of their rejecting Christ, in casting off whom they cast off God, that he should not reign over them. <div eID="gen5440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5441" type="x-p"/> II. He puts them upon choosing their king by lot. He knew whom God had chosen, and had already anointed him, but he knew also the peevishness of that people, and that there were those among them who would not acquiesce in the choice if it depended upon his single testimony; and therefore, that every tribe and every family of the chosen tribe might please themselves with having a chance for it, he calls them to the lot, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.19">v. 19</reference>. Benjamin is taken out of all the tribes (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.20">v. 20</reference>), and out of that tribe Saul the son of Kish, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.21">v. 21</reference>. By this method it would appear to the people, as it already appeared to Samuel, that Saul was appointed of God to be king; for <hi type="italic">the disposal of the lot is of the Lord.</hi> It would also prevent all disputes and exceptions; for <hi type="italic">the lot causeth contentions to cease, and parteth between the mighty.</hi> When the tribe of Benjamin was taken, they might easily foresee that they were setting up a family that would soon be put down again; for dying Jacob had, by the spirit of prophecy, entailed the dominion upon Judah. Judah is the tribe that must <hi type="italic">rule as a lion; Benjamin</hi> shall only <hi type="italic">ravin as a wolf,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen. xlix. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.27">27</reference>. Those therefore that knew the scriptures could not be very fond of the doing of that which they foresaw must, ere long, be undone again. <div eID="gen5441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5442" type="x-p"/> III. It is with much ado, and not without further enquiries of the Lord, that Saul is at length produced. When the lot fell upon him, every one expected he should answer to his name at the first call, but, instead of that, none of his friends could find him (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.21">v. 21</reference>), he had <hi type="italic">hidden himself among the stuff</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.22">v. 22</reference>), so little fond was he now of that power which yet, when he was in possession of, he could not without the utmost indignation think of parting with. <div eID="gen5442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5443" type="x-p"/> 1. He withdrew, in hopes that, upon his not appearing, they would proceed to another choice, or thus to express his modesty; for, by what had already passed, he knew he must be the man. We may suppose he was at this time really averse to take upon him the government, (1.) Because he was conscious to himself of unfitness for so great a trust. He had not been bred up to books, or arms, or courts, and feared he should be guilty of some fatal blunder. (2.) Because it would expose him to the envy of his neighbours that were ill-affected towards him. (3.) Because he understood, by what Samuel had said, that the people sinned in asking a king, and it was in anger that God granted their request. (4.) Because the affairs of Israel were at this time in a bad posture; the Philistines were strong, the Ammonites threatening: and he must be bold indeed that will set sail in a storm. <div eID="gen5443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5444" type="x-p"/> 2. But the congregation, believing that choice well made which God himself made, would leave no way untried to find him out on whom the lot fell. <hi type="italic">They enquired of the Lord,</hi> either by the high priest, and his breast-plate of judgment, or by Samuel, and his spirit of prophecy; and the Lord directed them where they should find him, hidden among the carriages, and thence <hi type="italic">they fetched him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.23">v. 23</reference>. Note, None will be losers at last by their humility and modesty. Honour, like the shadow, follows those that flee from it, but flees from those that pursue it. <div eID="gen5444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5445" type="x-p"/> IV. Samuel presents him to the people, and they accept him. He needed not to mount the bench, or scaffold, to be seen; when he stood upon even ground with the rest he was seen above them all, for he was taller than any of them by <hi type="italic">head and shoulders,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.23">v. 23</reference>. "Look you," said Samuel, "what a king God has chosen for you, just such a one as you wished for; <hi type="italic">there is none like him among all the people,</hi> that has so much majesty in his countenance and such a graceful stateliness in his mien; he is in the crowd like a cedar among the shrubs. Let your own eyes be judges, is he not a brave and gallant man?" The people hereupon signified their approbation of the choice, and their acceptance of him; they <hi type="italic">shouted and said, Let the king live,</hi> that is, "Let him long reign over us in health and prosperity." Subjects were wont to testify their affection and allegiance to their prince by their good wishes, and those turned (as our translation does this) into addresses to God. <reference osisRef="Ps.72.15">Ps. lxxii. 15</reference>, <hi type="italic">Prayer shall be made for him continually.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Ps.20.1">Ps. xx. 1</reference>. Samuel had told them they would soon be weary of their king, but, in the mind they are now in, they will never be so: <hi type="italic">Let the king live.</hi> <div eID="gen5445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5446" type="x-p"/> V. Samuel settles the original contract between them, and leaves it upon record, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.25">v. 25</reference>. He had before told them <hi type="italic">the manner of the king</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.8.11">ch. viii. 11</reference>), how he would abuse his power; now he tells them <hi type="italic">the manner of the kingdom,</hi> or rather the law, or judgment, or constitution, of it, what power the prince might challenge and the utmost of the property the subject might claim. He fixed the land-marks between them, that neither might encroach upon the other. Let them rightly understand one another at first, and let the agreement remain in black and white, which will tend to preserve a good understanding between them ever after. The learned bishop Patrick thinks he now repeated and registered what he had told them (<reference osisRef="1Sam.8.11">ch. viii. 11</reference>) of the arbitrary power their kings would assume, that it might hereafter be a witness against them that they had drawn the calamity upon themselves, for they were warned what it would come to and yet they would have a king. <div eID="gen5446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5447" type="x-p"/> VI. The convention was dissolved when the solemnity was over: <hi type="italic">Samuel sent every man to his house.</hi> Here were no votes passed, nor, for aught that appears, so much as a motion made, for the raising of money to support the dignity of their new-elected king; if therefore he afterwards thinks fit to take what they do not think fit to give (which yet it was necessary that he should have), they must thank themselves. They went every man to his house, pleased with the name of a king over them, and <hi type="italic">Saul also went home to Gibeah,</hi> to his father's house, not puffed up with the name of a kingdom under him. At Gibeah he had no palace, no throne, no court, yet thither he goes. If he must be a king, as one mindful of the rock out of which he was hewn, he will make his own city the royal city, nor will he be ashamed (as too many are when they are preferred) of his mean relations. Such a humble spirit as this puts a beauty and lustre upon great advancements. The condition rising, and the mind not rising with it, behold how good and pleasant it is! But, <div eID="gen5447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5448" type="x-p"/> 1. How did the people stand affected to their new king? The generality of them, it should seem, did not show themselves much concerned: They <hi type="italic">went every man to his own house.</hi> Their own domestic affairs lay nearer their hearts than any interests of the public; this was the general temper. But, (1.) There were some so faithful as to attend him: <hi type="italic">A band of men whose hearts God had touched,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.26">v. 26</reference>. Not the body of the people, but a small company, who because they were fond of their own choice of a king, or because they had so much more sense than their neighbours as to conclude that if he was a king he ought to be respected accordingly, went with him to Gibeah, as his life-guard. They were those <hi type="italic">whose hearts God had touched,</hi> in this instance, to do their duty. Note, Whatever good there is in us, or is done by us, at any time, it must be ascribed to the grace of God. If the heart bend at any time the right way, it is because he has touched it. One touch is enough, when it is divine. (2.) There were others so spiteful as to affront him; children of Belial, men that would endure no yoke, that would be pleased with nothing that either God or Samuel did; they <hi type="italic">despised him</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.27">v. 27</reference>) for the meanness of his tribe and family, the smallness of his estate, and the privacy of his education; and they said, <hi type="italic">How shall this man save us?</hi> Yet they did not propose any man more likely; nor, whomsoever they had, must their salvation come from the man, but from God. They would not join with their neighbours in testifying an affection to him and his government, by bringing him presents, or addressing him upon his accession to the crown. Perhaps those discontented spirits were most earnest for a king, and yet, now that they had one, they quarrelled with him, because he was not altogether such a one as themselves. It was reason enough for them not to like him because others did. Thus differently are men affected to our exalted Redeemer. God hath set him king upon the holy hill of Sion. There is a remnant that submit to him, rejoice in him, bring him presents, and follow him wherever he goes; and they are those <hi type="italic">whose hearts God has touched,</hi> whom he has <hi type="italic">made willing in the day of his power.</hi> But there are others who despise him, who ask, <hi type="italic">How shall this man save us?</hi> They are offended in him, stumble at his external meanness, and they will be broken by it. <div eID="gen5448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5449" type="x-p"/> 2. How did Saul resent the bad conduct of those that were disaffected to his government? <hi type="italic">He held his peace.</hi> Margin, <hi type="italic">He was as though he had been deaf.</hi> He was so far from resenting it that he seemed not to take notice of it, which was an evidence of his humility and modesty, and the mercifulness of his disposition, and also that he was well satisfied with his title to the crown; for those are commonly most jealous of their honour, and most revengeful of affronts, that gain their power by improper means. Christ held his peace when he was affronted, for it was the day of his patience; but there is a day of recompence coming.  <chapter eID="1Sam.10"/> <div eID="gen5449" type="x-p"/>

entries.f5385625f2e9107841f046beb1e39ebcdfc78f86: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2584"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 10</title> <div sID="gen3497" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.1-1Sam.10.27">1Sa 10:1-27</reference>. Samuel Anoints Saul, and Confirms Him by the Prediction of Three Signs.<div eID="gen3497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3498" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2584"/><hi type="bold">1. Then Samuel took a vial of oil--</hi>This was the ancient (<reference osisRef="Judg.9.8">Jud 9:8</reference>) ceremony of investiture with the royal office among the Hebrews and other Eastern nations. But there were two unctions to the kingly office; the one in private, by a prophet (<reference osisRef="1Sam.16.13">1Sa 16:13</reference>), which was meant to be only a prophetic intimation of the person attaining that high dignity--the more public and formal inauguration (<reference osisRef="2Sam.2.4">2Sa 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.3">5:3</reference>) was performed by the high priest, and perhaps with the holy oil, but that is not certain. The first of a dynasty was thus anointed, but not his heirs, unless the succession was disputed (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.39">1Ki 1:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.11.12">2Ki 11:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.30">23:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.23.11">2Ch 23:11</reference>).<div eID="gen3498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3499" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kissed him--</hi>This salutation, as explained by the words that accompanied it, was an act of respectful homage, a token of congratulation to the new king (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.12">Psa 2:12</reference>). <div eID="gen3499" type="x-p"/>
entries.893cbf8f5be1e1d6c3638da8a77c49a95fe4a1b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2585"/><div sID="gen3500" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2585"/><hi type="bold">2. When thou art departed from me to-day--</hi>The design of these specific predictions of what should be met with on the way, and the number and minuteness of which would arrest attention, was to confirm Saul's reliance on the prophetic character of Samuel, and lead him to give full credence to what had been revealed to him as the word of God.<div eID="gen3500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3501" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Rachel's sepulchre--</hi>near Beth-lehem (see on <reference osisRef="Gen.35.16">Ge 35:16</reference>).<div eID="gen3501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3502" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zelzah--</hi>or Zelah, now Bet-jalah, in the neighborhood of that town. <div eID="gen3502" type="x-p"/>
entries.709885b2ab89124fdb96d04cc5eb0d54d51ec45e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2586"/><div sID="gen3503" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2586"/><hi type="bold">3. the plain--</hi>or, "the oak of Tabor," not the celebrated mount, for that was far distant.<div eID="gen3503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3504" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">three men going up to God to Beth-el--</hi>apparently to offer sacrifices there at a time when the ark and the tabernacle were not in a settled abode, and God had not yet declared the permanent place which He should choose. The kids were for sacrifice, the loaves for the offering, and the wine for the libations. <div eID="gen3504" type="x-p"/>
entries.31943fc8186bc0a93ce7336905ad42d2faec06e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2587"/><div sID="gen3505" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2587"/><hi type="bold">5. the hill of God--</hi>probably Geba (<reference osisRef="1Sam.13.3">1Sa 13:3</reference>), so called from a school of the prophets being established there. The company of prophets were, doubtless, the pupils at this seminary, which had probably been instituted by Samuel, and in which the chief branches of education taught were a knowledge of the law, and of psalmody with instrumental music, which is called "prophesying" (here and in <reference osisRef="1Chr.25.1">1Ch 25:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.25.7">7</reference>). <div eID="gen3505" type="x-p"/>
entries.a03908d7c5944dfa5107ce4a8c187fb592b45129: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2588"/><div sID="gen3506" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2588"/><hi type="bold">6. the Spirit of the Lord will come upon thee--</hi>literally, "rush upon thee," suddenly endowing thee with a capacity and disposition to act in a manner far superior to thy previous character and habits; and instead of the simplicity, ignorance, and sheepishness of a peasant, thou wilt display an energy, wisdom, and magnanimity worthy of a prince. <div eID="gen3506" type="x-p"/>
entries.b70140cce96a7c1c9662894c4ee36f22f88fd788: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2589"/><div sID="gen3507" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2589"/><hi type="bold">8. thou shalt go down before me to Gilgal--</hi>This, according to Josephus, was to be a standing rule for the observance of Saul while the prophet and he lived; that in every great crisis, such as a hostile incursion on the country, he should repair to Gilgal, where he was to remain seven days, to afford time for the tribes on both sides Jordan to assemble, and Samuel to reach it. <div eID="gen3507" type="x-p"/>
entries.f1d4a85ca09c49e5d87b33558e319711f6faf6ac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2590"/><div sID="gen3508" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2590"/><hi type="bold">9-11. when he had turned his back to go from Samuel, God gave him another heart--</hi>Influenced by the words of Samuel, as well as by the accomplishment of these signs, Saul's reluctance to undertake the onerous office was overcome. The fulfilment of the two first signs [1Sa 10:7, 8] is passed over, but the third is specially described. The spectacle of a man, though more fit to look after his father's cattle than to take part in the sacred exercises of the young prophets--a man without any previous instruction, or any known taste, entering with ardor into the spirit, and skilfully accompanying the melodies of the sacred band, was so extraordinary a phenomenon, that it gave rise to the proverb, "Is Saul also among the prophets?" (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.24">1Sa 19:24</reference>). The prophetic spirit had come upon him; and to Saul it was as personal and experimental an evidence of the truth of God's word that had been spoken to him, as converts to Christianity have in themselves from the sanctifying power of the Gospel. <div eID="gen3508" type="x-p"/>
entries.428ba9c437db1467141783be494d43eb95134fec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2591"/><div sID="gen3509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2591"/><hi type="bold">12. But who is their father?--</hi>The Septuagint reads, "Who is his father?" referring to Saul the son of Kish. <div eID="gen3509" type="x-p"/>
entries.d0f6f9dbb9b19c5cec18259cfbb93d0f746658ae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2592"/><div sID="gen3510" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2592"/><hi type="bold">17-25. Samuel called the people together ... at Mizpeh--</hi>a shaft-like hill near Hebron, five hundred feet in height. The national assemblies of the Israelites were held there. A day having been appointed for the election of a king, Samuel, after having charged the people with a rejection of God's institution and a superseding of it by one of their own, proceeded to the nomination of the new monarch. As it was of the utmost importance that the appointment should be under the divine direction and control, the determination was made by the miraculous lot, tribes, families, and individuals being successively passed until Saul was found. His concealment of himself must have been the result either of innate modesty, or a sudden nervous excitement under the circumstances. When dragged into view, he was seen to possess all those corporeal advantages which a rude people desiderate in their sovereigns; and the exhibition of which gained for the prince the favorable opinion of Samuel also. In the midst of the national enthusiasm, however, the prophet's deep piety and genuine patriotism took care to explain "the manner of the kingdom," that is, the royal rights and privileges, together with the limitations to which they were to be subjected; and in order that the constitution might be ratified with all due solemnity, the charter of this constitutional monarchy was recorded and laid up "before the Lord," that is, deposited in the custody of the priests, along with the most sacred archives of the nation. <div eID="gen3510" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9ea42bbd778f3e971860c2d382ecee378044ba1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2593"/><div sID="gen3511" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2593"/><hi type="bold">26. And Saul also went home to Gibeah--</hi>near Geba. This was his place of residence (see <reference osisRef="Judg.20.20">Jud 20:20</reference>), about five miles north of Jerusalem.<div eID="gen3511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there went ... a band of men, whose hearts God had touched--</hi>who feared God and regarded allegiance to their king as a conscientious duty. They are opposed to "the children of Belial." <div eID="gen3512" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e2dd8d7052520a737bc3f5500d21d0936afe10f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2594"/><div sID="gen3513" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2594"/><hi type="bold">27. the children of Belial said, How shall this man save us? And they despised him, and brought him no presents--</hi>In Eastern countries, the honor of the sovereign and the splendor of the royal household are upheld, not by a fixed rate of taxation, but by presents brought at certain seasons by officials, and men of wealth, from all parts of the kingdom, according to the means of the individual, and of a customary registered value. Such was the tribute which Saul's opponents withheld, and for want of which he was unable to set up a kingly establishment for a while. But "biding his time," he bore the insult with a prudence and magnanimity which were of great use in the beginning of his government. <chapter eID="1Sam.10"/>

entries.ffb5892c70435ae94017ca103a183aa75d4e6ee3: <div eID="gen9897" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen9898" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9899" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9899" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9898" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9900" type="x-p"/> Samuel anoints Saul captain of the Lord's inheritance, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.1">1Sam 10:1</reference>. Instructs him concerning his return home, whom he should meet, and what he should do, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.2-1Sam.10.8">1Sam 10:2-8</reference>. Saul meets a company of prophets, the Spirit of the Lord comes on him, and he prophesies among them, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.9-1Sam.10.13">1Sam 10:9-13</reference>. He meets his uncle, and converses with him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.14-1Sam.10.16">1Sam 10:14-16</reference>. Samuel calls the people together to Mizpeh, and upbraids them for having rejected the Lord as their king, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.17-1Sam.10.19">1Sam 10:17-19</reference>. Lots are cast to find out the person proper to be appointed king; Saul is chosen, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.20-1Sam.10.24">1Sam 10:20-24</reference>. Samuel shows the manner of the king, and writes it in a book, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.25">1Sam 10:25</reference>. Saul goes to Gibeah; and certain persons refuse to acknowledge him as king, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.26">1Sam 10:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.27">1Sam 10:27</reference>. <div eID="gen9900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9901" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen9901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9902" type="x-p"/> Took a vial of oil - The reasons of this rite the reader will find largely stated in the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.29.7">Exo 29:7</reference>. The anointing mentioned here took place in the open field. See the preceding chapter, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.26-1Sam.9.27">1Sam 9:26-27</reference> (note). How simple was the ancient ceremony of consecrating a king! A prophet or priest poured oil upon his head, and kissed him; and said, Thus the Lord hath anointed thee to be captain over his inheritance. This was the whole of the ceremony. Even in this anointing, Saul is not acknowledged as king, but simply נגיד nagid, a captain - one who goes before and leads the people.
entries.54201af334f64a5ceae208fc5da0ad0fae13291e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen9902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9903" type="x-p"/> Rachel's sepulcher - This was nigh to Bethlehem. See <reference osisRef="Gen.35.19">Gen 35:19</reference>. <div eID="gen9903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9904" type="x-p"/> At Zelzah - If this be the name of a place, nothing is known of it. <div eID="gen9904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9905" type="x-p"/> The Hebrew בצלצח betseltsach is translated by the Septuagint ἁλλομενους μεγαλα, dancing greatly: now this may refer to the joy they felt and expressed on finding the asses, or it may refer to those religious exultations, or playing on instruments of music, mentioned in the succeeding verses.
entries.28192cd8f974fb70eac28ff1168fdce582b88aa7: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen9905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9906" type="x-p"/> Three men going up to God to Bethel - Jacob's altar was probably there still, <reference osisRef="Gen.28.19">Gen 28:19</reference>. However this might be, it was still considered, as its name implies, the house of God; and to it they were now going, to offer sacrifice. <div eID="gen9906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9907" type="x-p"/> The three kids were for sacrifice; the three loaves of bread to be offered probably as a thank-offering; and the bottle or skin full of wine, for a libation. When the blood was poured out before the Lord, then they feasted on the flesh and on the bread; and probably had a sufficiency of the wine left for their own drinking.
entries.1ccc0c3066e89746810a2c1e7bf1cc0f2d8f9251: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen9907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9908" type="x-p"/> And they will salute thee - ושאלו לך לשלום veshaalu lecha leshalom, "And they will inquire of thee concerning peace," i.e., welfare. In the East, if this salutation be given, then the person or persons giving it may be reckoned friends; if the others return it, then there is friendship on both sides. Salaam alicum, Peace to you! is the mode of compellation: Alicum essalaam, To you be peace! is the return. If you give the former and receive not the latter, you may expect hostility. The meaning of the prophet is, When you come to the plain of Tabor, ye shall meet three men; you need not be afraid of them, for they are friends; and they will show this friendship, not only by bidding you good speed, but by giving you two loaves of bread, a provision which you will need for the remaining part of your journey.
entries.e15ab549fe6d7e8e46d33dc9e8930cf46edc4e53: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen9908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9909" type="x-p"/> The hill of God - The Targum says, "The hill on which the ark of the Lord was. Calmet supposes it to be a height near Gibeah. <div eID="gen9909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9910" type="x-p"/> The garrison of the Philistines - Probably they kept a watch on the top of this hill, with a company of soldiers to keep the country in check. <div eID="gen9910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9911" type="x-p"/> A company of prophets - A company of scribes, says the Targum. Probably the scholars of the prophets; for the prophets seem to have been the only accredited teachers, at particular times, in Israel; and at this time there does not appear to have been any other prophet besides Samuel in this quarter. Probably the teacher of this school was not an inspired man, but one acting under the direction of Samuel. Mr. Harmer thinks that the following custom among the Mohammedans greatly illustrates this obscure place: "When the children have gone through the Koran, their relations borrow a fine horse and furniture, and carry them about the town in procession, with the book in their hand, the rest of their companions following, and all sorts of music of the country going before. Dr. Shaw, in p. 195, mentions the same custom; adding the acclamations of their school-fellows, but taking no notice of the music. We have no reason, however, to doubt the fact on account of the doctor's silence; especially as it relates to another part of Barbary, and is given us by those who resided some years in that country. The doctor makes no use of this circumstance relating to the education of youth in Barbary; but the account of the procession above given seems to be a lively comment on that ancient Jewish custom mentioned in these verses. That the word prophet often signifies sons or scholars of the prophets, and that prophesying often implies singing, has been already remarked; but no author that I know of has given any account of the nature of this procession, or its design. We are sometimes told that high places were used for sacrifices; and in one case music, it is certain, played before them when they went up to worship, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.29">Isa 30:29</reference>. But did they not also return from sacrifice with it? We are told that music was used by the prophets to calm and compose them, and to invite the Divine influences; which is indeed very true. But is it to the purpose? Did they go forth in this manner from their college into the noise and interruptions of the world, to call down the prophetic impulse? But if we consider them as a company of the sons of the prophets, going in procession with songs of praise and music playing before them, and recollect that it is usual in this day for young scholars to go in procession with acclamations and music, the whole mystery seems to be unravelled. To which may be added, that Saul was to meet them, and find himself turned into another man; into a man, perhaps, who is instantaneously made as knowing in the law of God as the youth to whom they were doing the above honors, or any of his convoy; which acquaintance with the law of God was very necessary for one who was to judge among his brethren as their king. For this reason the Jewish kings were to write out a copy of the law of God, and read it continually, that they might be perfect masters of it, <reference osisRef="Deu.17.18">Deu 17:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.17.20">Deu 17:20</reference>, which accomplishment some youth had gained whom Saul met with, and who was honored with the solemnity the sacred historian speaks of, if the customs of South Barbary may be supposed to be explanatory of those of Judea." <div eID="gen9911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9912" type="x-p"/> On the word prophet, and the general account given here, I shall introduce the following illustrations from another work: - "The word prophet generally conveys the idea of a person so far acquainted with futurity as to discern some purpose of the Divine Being relative to his government of the natural and moral world, but which is not sufficiently matured by the economy of Providence to make, as yet, its public appearance among men, and to prophesy is usually understood to imply the foretelling such an event, the time of its appearance, and the place of its operation, with some preceding and subsequent circumstances. But that this was the original and only meaning of the word prophet or prophesy, is very far from being clear. The first place the word occurs in is <reference osisRef="Gen.20.7">Gen 20:7</reference>, where the Lord says of Abraham to Abimelech, He is a prophet, (נביא הוא nabi hu), and will pray (ויתפלל veyith-pallel, will make earnest intercession) for thee. In the common acceptation of the word it is certain Abraham was no prophet; but here it seems to signify a man well acquainted with the Supreme Being, capable of teaching others in Divine things, and especially a man of prayer - one who had great influence with the God he worshipped, and whose intercessions were available in the behalf of others. And in this sense the original word נביא nabi is used in several places in the Old Testament. "It was through inattention to this meaning of the word, which appears to me to be the true, original, and ideal one, that all the commentators and critics that I have met with have been so sadly puzzled with that part of the history of Saul which is related <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.9-1Sam.10.13">1Sam 10:9-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.20-1Sam.19.24">1Sam 19:20-24</reference>. In these passages the sacred historian represents Saul, who was neither a prophet nor the son of one, associating with the prophets, and prophesying among them, to which he was led by the Spirit of the Lord which came upon him. "That this can mean no more here than prayer and supplication to God, accompanied probably with edifying hymns of praise and thanksgiving, (for they had instruments of music, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.5">1Sam 10:5</reference>), needs, in my opinion, little proof. If Saul had prophesied in the common acceptation of the word, it is not likely that we should have been kept absolutely in the dark concerning the subject and design of his predictions, of which, by the way, not one syllable is spoken in the oracles of God. The simple fact seems to have been this: God, who had chosen this man to govern Israel, designed to teach him that the Most High alone is the fountain of power, and that by him only kings could reign so as to execute justice properly, and be his ministers for good to the people. To accomplish this gracious purpose, he gave him another heart (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.9">1Sam 10:9</reference>)-a disposition totally different from what he had ever before possessed, and taught him to pray. "Coming among the sons of the prophets, on whom the Spirit of the Lord rested, and who were under the instruction of Samuel, (<reference osisRef="1Sam.19.20">1Sam 19:20</reference>), while they worshipped God with music and supplication, Saul also was made a partaker of the same Divine influence, and prophesied, i.e., made prayer and supplication among them. To see one who did not belong to the prophetic school thus incorporated with the prophets, pouring out his soul in prayer and supplication, was an unusual sight, which could not pass unnoticed, especially by those of Saul's acquaintance who probably knew him in times past to have been as careless and ungodly as themselves, (for it was only now he got that other good Spirit from God, a sufficient proof that he had it not before). These companions of his, being unacquainted with that grace which can in a moment influence and change the heart, would, according to an invariable custom, express their astonishment with a sneer: Is Saul also among the prophets? That is, in modern language, 'Can this man pray or preach? He whose education has been the same as our own, employed in the same secular offices, and formerly companion with us in what he now affects to call folly and sin? Can such a person be among the prophets?' Yes, for God may have given him a new heart; and the Spirit of God, whose inspiration alone can give sound understanding in sacred things, may have come upon him for this very purpose, that he might announce unto you the righteousness of the Lord, and speak unto your ruined souls to edification, and to exhortation, and to comfort. "The history of Elijah and the priests of Baal, mentioned in 1 Kings 18:17-40, throws farther light on this subject. In <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.26">1Kgs 18:26</reference> it is said, 'They (the priests of Baal) took a bullock and dressed it, and called on the name of Baal, from morning to noon, saying, O Baal, hear us! And they leaped upon the altar, and cried aloud, and cut themselves with knives, till the blood gushed out; and they prophesied (ויתנבאו vaiyithnabbeu, and they made supplication) until the time of the evening sacrifice.' From the whole context it is plain that earnest, importunate prayer, is alone what is meant by prophesying in this text. See also <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.3">1Cor 14:3</reference> (note). "And as all the prophets of God, whose principal business it was to instruct the people in the way of righteousness, were men of prayer, who were continually interceding with God in behalf of those to whom they ministered, the term נביא nabi became their proper appellative; and thus a part of their office, intercessors for the people, might have given rise to that name by which the Spirit of God thought proper in after times to distinguish those whom he sent, not only to pray for and instruct the people, but also to predict those future events which concerned the punishment of the incorrigible and the comfort and exaltation of his own servants." See a sermon which I have printed on <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.3">1Cor 14:3</reference>, entitled, "The Christian Prophet and his Work;" and see the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.20.7">Gen 20:7</reference>. <div eID="gen9912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9913" type="x-p"/> A psaltery - נבל nebel. As the word signifies in other places a bottle or flagon, it was probably something like the utricularia tibia or Bag-Pipe. It often occurs both with the Greeks and Romans, and was evidently borrowed from the Hebrews. <div eID="gen9913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9914" type="x-p"/> A tabret - תף toph; a sort of drum or cymbal. <div eID="gen9914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9915" type="x-p"/> A pipe - חליל chalil, from חל chal, to make a hole or opening; a sort of pipe, flute, hautboy, clarionet, or the like. <div eID="gen9915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9916" type="x-p"/> A harp - כנור kinnor; a stringed instrument similar to our harp, or that on the model of which a harp was formed. On these different instruments I shall have occasion to speak more at large when I come to the Psalms.
entries.130683655d30965eb251cc46fb1586d0ef9c5797: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen9916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9917" type="x-p"/> Thou do as occasion serve thee - After God has shown thee all these signs that thou art under his especial guidance, fear not to undertake any thing that belongs to thy office, for God is with thee. <div eID="gen9917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9918" type="x-p"/> What a number of circumstances thus precisely foretold! Does not this prove that Samuel was under the continual inspiration of the Almighty?
entries.f7a75a411c776fcca93d9ea930e41785111bb2a6: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen9918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9919" type="x-p"/> Seven days shalt thou tarry - I will come to thee within seven days, offer sacrifices, receive directions from the Lord, and deliver them to thee. It is likely that these seven days referred to the time in which Samuel came to Saul to Gilgal, offered sacrifices, and confirmed the kingdom to him, after he had defeated the Ammonites. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.14">1Sam 11:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.15">1Sam 11:15</reference>.
entries.9dff40696384d54aa3e8b8d183ee1214800ede7e: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen9919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9920" type="x-p"/> Behold, a company of prophets - See on <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.5">1Sam 10:5</reference> (note), etc.
entries.48fa9038fb7cf3e86152e4f5a96d9956fe8b739d: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen9920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9921" type="x-p"/> But who is their father? - The Septuagint, in its principal editions, adds ου Κεις; is it not Kish? This makes the sense more complete.
entries.5d7a207c18d8ded2a6840d1b4d4b6718cb0223ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen9921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9922" type="x-p"/> He came to the high place - I suppose this to mean the place where Saul's father lived; as it is evident the next verse shows him to be at home.
entries.58ff086569549212d54556e197983755a006946d: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen9922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9923" type="x-p"/> Saul's uncle - The word דוד dod signifies a beloved one, love, a lover, friend, etc.; and is the same as David. It is supposed to mean uncle here; but I think it means some familiar friend.
entries.bd84f08c327bb5fc401cc6d58442c68f654eac2e: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen9923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9924" type="x-p"/> I brought up Israel out of Egypt - These are similar to the upbraidings in <reference osisRef="1Sam.8.7">1Sam 8:7</reference>, etc.
entries.39dcb60f0912b04b07103ba24114b9f9626a1a8b: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen9924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9925" type="x-p"/> Present yourselves - by your tribes - It appears that, in order to find out the proper person who should be made their king, they must determine by lot: <div eID="gen9925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9926" type="x-p"/> 1. The tribe. <div eID="gen9926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9927" type="x-p"/> 2. The thousands or grand divisions by families. <div eID="gen9927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9928" type="x-p"/> 3. The smaller divisions by families. And, <div eID="gen9928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9929" type="x-p"/> 4. The individual. <div eID="gen9929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9930" type="x-p"/> When the lot was cast for the tribe, Benjamin was taken; when for the thousand, the division of Matri was taken; when for the family, the family of Kish was taken; when for the individual, Saul, the son of Kish, was taken.
entries.66af937942c3e51693302fdbf9102b2e0e599182: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen9930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9931" type="x-p"/> When they sought him, he could not be found - Through modesty or fear he had secreted himself.
entries.4efbe71941fc15ebd28b163e5eb663e96849acde: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen9931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9932" type="x-p"/> The Lord answered - What a continual access to God! and what condescension in his attention to all their requests! <div eID="gen9932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9933" type="x-p"/> The stuff among which he had secreted himself may mean the carts, baggage, etc., brought by the people to Mizpeh.
entries.d8f349981b26cff38450b16f84b298bc4ccef048: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen9933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9934" type="x-p"/> God save the king - There is no such word here; no, nor in the whole Bible; nor is it countenanced by any of the versions. The words which we thus translate here and elsewhere are simply יחי המלך yechi hammelech, "May the king live;" and so all the versions, the Targum excepted, which says, May the king prosper! The French Vive le roi! is a proper version of the Hebrew.
entries.59b2b5deb2af355f109dc4133e4841f622079bc9: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen9934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9935" type="x-p"/> The manner of the kingdom - It is the same word as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.8.9">1Sam 8:9</reference>; and doubtless the same thing is implied as is there related. But possibly there was some kind of compact or covenant between them and Saul; and this was the thing that was written in a book, and laid up before the Lord, probably near the ark.
entries.77830695527549ba96c7adedc8cf7dfec8c5b61f: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen9935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9936" type="x-p"/> A band of men - Not a military band, as I imagine, but some secret friends, or companions, who were personally attached to him. Others think that all the men fit to bear arms are intended; but this seems inconsistent with the life that Saul led for some time afterwards; for he appears to have gone into his agricultural concerns, and waited for a call from the Divine providence. See <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.5">1Sam 11:5</reference>.
entries.c3dbdf9a41f0df8e16d18f64b82b60e4b6e8c64d: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen9936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9937" type="x-p"/> Brought him no presents - They gave him no proofs that they acknowledged either the Divine appointment or his authority. The Arab chiefs are, to this day, when on a march or excursion of any kind, supplied with every necessary by the free-will offerings or presents of the people in the villages or places where they encamp. Saul was now a public character, and had a right to support from the public. These sons of Belial refused to bear their part; they brought him no presents. He marked it, but at present held his peace; he was as if he were deaf: so says the text. He was prudent, and did not immediately assume all the consequence to which his office entitled him. It is probable, however, that tribute is meant by the word present. The people in general finding they had now a king, took it for granted that they must pay tribute or taxes to him. This was a part of the manner of the king which Samuel had shown them; the great majority had done so, but certain refractory people refused to pay any thing, on the pretense that such a person as Saul could not be a deliverer of Israel. How, say they, shall this man save us?  <chapter eID="1Sam.10"/> <div eID="gen9937" type="x-p"/>

entries.68d27b56a4271a2ab830e4ae73c682231464a324: <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.1">1Sa 10:1</reference> <div eID="gen3783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3784" type="x-p"/> Samuel then took the oil-flask, poured it upon his (Saul’s) head, kissed him, and said, “<hi type="italic">Hath not Jehovah</hi> (equivalent to 'Jehovah assuredly hath') <hi type="italic">anointed thee to be captain over His inheritance?</hi>” הלוא, as an expression of lively assurance, receives the force of an independent clause through the following כּי, “<hi type="italic">is it not so?</hi>” i.e., “yea, it is so, that,” etc., just as it does before אם in Gen 4:7. נחלתו, (His (Jehovah’s) possession, was the nation of Israel, which Jehovah had acquired as the people of His own possession through their deliverance out of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.20">Deu 4:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.9.26">Deu 9:26</reference>, etc.). Anointing with oil as a symbol of endowment with the Spirit of God; as the oil itself, by virtue of the strength which it gives to the vital spirits, was a symbol of the Spirit of God as the principle of divine and spiritual power (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.8.12">Lev 8:12</reference>). Hitherto there had been no other anointing among the people of God than that of the priests and sanctuary (Exo 30:23.; Lev 8:10.). When Saul, therefore, was consecrated as king by anointing, the monarchy was inaugurated as a divine institution, standing on a par with the priesthood; through which henceforth the Lord would also bestow upon His people the gifts of His Spirit for the building up of His kingdom. As the priests were consecrated by anointing to be the media of the ethical blessings of divine grace for Israel, so the king was consecrated by anointing to be the vehicle and medium of all the blessings of grace which the Lord, as the God-king, would confer upon His people through the institution of a civil government. Through this anointing, which was performed by Samuel under the direction of God, the king was set apart from the rest of the nation as “anointed of the Lord” (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.3">1Sa 12:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.5">1Sa 12:5</reference>, etc.), and sanctified as the נגיד, i.e., its captain, its leader and commander. <hi type="italic">Kissing</hi> was probably not a sign of homage or reverence towards the anointed of the Lord, so much as “a kiss of affection, with which the grace of God itself was sealed” (Seb. Schmidt).<note placement="foot">The lxx and Vulgate have expanded the second half of this verse by a considerable addition, which reads as follows in the lxx: οὐχὶ κέχρικέ σε κύριος εἰς ἄρχοντα ἐπὶ τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ Ἰσραήλ καὶ σὺ ἄρξεις ἐν λαῷ κυρίου, καὶ σὺ σώσεις αὐτὸν ἐκ χειρὸς ἐχθρῶν αὐτοῦ κυκλόθεν, καὶ τοῦτό σοι τὸ σημεῖον ὅτι ἔχρισέ σε κύριος ἐπὶ κληρονομίαν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἄρχοντα. And in the Vulgate: <hi type="italic">Ecce, unxit te Dominus super haereditatem suam in principem, et liberabis populum suum de manibus inimicorum ejus, qui in circuitu ejus sunt. Et hoc tibi signum, quia unxit te Deus in principem.</hi> A comparison of these two texts will show that the lxx interpolated their addition between הלוא and כּי, as the last clause, ὅτι ἔχρισέ σε κύριος ἐπὶ κληρονομίαν αυτοῦ εἰς ἄρχοντα, is a verbal translation of יהוה משׁחך כּי לנגיד על־נחלתו. In the Vulgate, on the other hand, the first clause, <hi type="italic">ecce unxit - in principem</hi>, corresponds word for word with the Hebrew text, from which we may see that <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi> translated our present Hebrew text; and the addition, <hi type="italic">et liberabis</hi>, etc., was interpolated into the Vulgate from the Itala. The text of the Septuagint is nothing more than a gloss formed from <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.16-1Sam.9.17">1Sa 9:16-17</reference>, which the translator thought necessary, partly because he could not clearly see the force of כּי הלוא, but more especially because he could not explain the fact that Samuel speaks to Saul of signs, without having announced them to him as such. But the author of the gloss has overlooked the fact that Samuel does not give Saul a σημεῖον, but three σημεῖα, and describes the object of them in <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.7">1Sa 10:7</reference> as being the following, namely, that Saul would learn when they took place what he had to do, for Jehovah was with him, and not that they would prove that the Lord had anointed him to be captain.</note> <div eID="gen3784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3785" type="x-p"/> To confirm the consecration of Saul as king over Israel, which had been effected through the anointing, Samuel gave him three more signs which would occur on his journey home, and would be a pledge to him that Jehovah would accompany his undertakings with His divine help, and practically accredit him as His anointed. These signs, therefore, stand in the closest relation to the calling conveyed to Saul through his anointing.
entries.748fa0a1ce96dec1c1f3fc22a2f51a1c3f49729c: <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.2">1Sa 10:2</reference> <hi type="italic">The first sign:</hi> “<hi type="italic">When thou goest away from me to-day </hi>(i.e., now),<hi type="italic">thou wilst meet two men at Rachel’s sepulchre, on the border of Benjamin at Zelzah; and they will say unto thee, The asses of thy father, which thou wentest to seek, are found. Behold, they father hath given up</hi> העתנות את־דּברי, <hi type="italic">the words</hi> (i.e., talking) <hi type="italic">about the asses, and troubleth himself about you, saying, What shall I do about my son?</hi>” According to Gen 35:16., Rachel’s sepulchre was on the way from Bethel to Bethlehem, only a short distance from the latter place, and therefore undoubtedly on the spot which tradition has assigned to it since the time of <hi type="italic">Jerome</hi>, viz., on the site of the <hi type="italic">Kubbet Rahil</hi>, half an hour to the north-west of Bethlehem, on the left of the road to Jerusalem, about an hour and a half from the city (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.35.20">Gen 35:20</reference>). This suits the passage before us very well, if we give up the groundless assumption that Saul came to Samuel at Ramah and was anointed by him there, and assume that the place of meeting, which is not more fully defined in 1 Samuel 9, was situated to the south-west of Bethlehem.<note placement="foot">As the account of Saul’s meeting with Samuel, in 1 Samuel 9, when properly understood, is not at variance with the tradition concerning the situation of Rachel’s tomb, and the passage before us neither requires us on the one had to understand the Ephratah of <reference osisRef="Gen.35.19">Gen 35:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.48.7">Gen 48:7</reference> as a different place from Bethlehem, and erase “<hi type="italic">that is Bethlehem</hi>” from both passages as a gloss that has crept into the text, and then invent an <hi type="italic">Ephratah</hi> in the neighbourhood of Bethel between Benjamin and Ephraim, as Thenius does, nor warrants us on the other hand in transferring Rachel’s tomb to the neighbourhood of Bethel, in opposition to the ordinary tradition, as Kurtz proposes; so the words of <reference osisRef="Jer.31.15">Jer 31:15</reference>, “A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation and bitter weeping, Rachel weeping for her children,” etc., furnish no evident that Rachel’s tomb was at Ramah (i.e., <hi type="italic">er Râm</hi>). “For here (in the cycle of prophecy concerning the restoration of all Israel, Jer 30-33) Rachel’s weeping is occasioned by the fact of the exiles of Benjamin having assembled together in Ramah (<reference osisRef="Jer.40.1">Jer 40:1</reference>), without there being any reason why Rachel’s tomb should be sought for in the neighbourhood of this Ramah” (Delitzsch on <reference osisRef="Gen.35.20">Gen 35:20</reference>).</note> <div eID="gen3785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3786" type="x-p"/> The expression “in the border of Benjamin” is not at variance with this.
