It is true that <hi type="italic">Kubbet Rahil</hi> is about an hour and a quarter from the southern boundary of Benjamin, which ran past the <hi type="italic">Rogel</hi> spring, through the valley of Ben-hinnom (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.16">Jos 18:16</reference>); but the expression קבוּרה עם must not be so pressed as to be restricted to the actual site of the grave, since otherwise the further definition “<hi type="italic">at Zelzah</hi>” would be superfluous, as Rachel’s tomb was unquestionably a well-known locality at that time. If we suppose the place called Zelzah, the situation of which has not yet been discovered,<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> (<hi type="italic">Gesch. </hi>iii. p. 29) supposes Zelzah to be unsuitable to the context, if taken as the name of a place, and therefore follows the ἁλλομένους μεγάλα of the lxx, and renders the word “in great haste;” but he has neither given any reason why the name of a place is unsuitable here, nor considered that the Septuagint rendering is merely conjectural, and has nothing further to support it than the fact that the translators rendered צלח ἐφήλατο, “he sprang upon him,” in <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.6">1Sa 10:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.6">1Sa 11:6</reference>, and took צלצח to be an emphatic form of צלח.</note> to have been about mid-way between Rachel’s tomb and the <hi type="italic">Rogel</hi> spring, Samuel could very well describe the spot where Saul would meet the two men in the way that he has done. This sign, by confirming the information which Samuel had given to Saul with reference to the asses, was to furnish him with a practical proof that what Samuel had said to him with regard to the monarchy would quite as certainly come to pass, and therefore not only to deliver him from all anxiety as to the lost animals of his father, but also to direct his thoughts to the higher destiny to which God had called him through Samuel’s anointing.
entries.c23bf76d08e3d054d5280bdcdf074dfd30d22c43: <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.3-1Sam.10.4">1Sa 10:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen3786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3787" type="x-p"/> The second sign (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.3">1Sa 10:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.4">1Sa 10:4</reference>): “<hi type="italic">Then thou shalt go on forward from thence, and thou shalt come to the terebinth of Tabor; and there shall meet thee there three men going up to God to Bethel, carrying one three kinds, one three loaves of bread, and one a bottle of wine. They will ask thee after thy welfare, and give thee two loaves; receive them at their hands</hi>.” The terebinth of <hi type="italic">Tabor </hi>is not mentioned anywhere else, and nothing further can be determined concerning it, than that it stood by the road leading from Rachel’s tomb to Gibeah.<note placement="foot">The opinion expressed by <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> and Thenius, that Deborah’s mourning oak (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.8">Gen 35:8</reference>) is intended, and that <hi type="italic">Tabor</hi> is either a different form of <hi type="italic">Deborah</hi>, or that <hi type="italic">Tabor</hi> should be altered into Deborah, has no foundation to rest upon; for the fact that the oak referred to stood below (i.e., to the south of) Bethel, and the three men whom Saul was to meet at the terebinth of <hi type="italic">Tabor</hi> were going to Bethel, by no means establishes the identity of the two, as their going up to Bethel does not prove that they were already in the neighbourhood of Bethel. Moreover, the Deborah oak was on the north of Gibeah, whereas Saul met the three men between Rachel’s tomb and Gibeah, i.e., to the south of Gibeah.</note> <div eID="gen3787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3788" type="x-p"/> The fact that the three men were going up to God at Bethel, shows that there was still a place of sacrifice consecrated to the Lord at Bethel, where Abraham and Jacob had erected altars to the Lord who had appeared to them there (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.8">Gen 12:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.13.3-Gen.13.4">Gen 13:3-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.28.18-Gen.28.19">Gen 28:18-19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.35.7">Gen 35:7</reference>); for the kids and loaves and wine were sacrificial gifts which they were about to offer. לשׁלום שׁאל, to ask after one’s welfare, i.e., to greet in a friendly manner (cf. Jdg 18:15; <reference osisRef="Gen.43.27">Gen 43:27</reference>). The meaning of this double sign consisted in the fact that these men gave Saul two loaves from their sacrificial offerings. In this he was to discern a homage paid to the anointed of the Lord; and he was therefore to accept the gift in this sense at their hand.
entries.97a07fc5f2d49d51139989aecb65cf71e9229398: <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.5-1Sam.10.6">1Sa 10:5-6</reference> <hi type="italic">The third sign</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.5">1Sa 10:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.6">1Sa 10:6</reference>) Saul was to receive at Gibeah of God, where posts of the Philistines were stationed. <hi type="italic">Gibeath ha-Elohim</hi> is not an appellative, signifying a high place of God, i.e., a high place dedicated to God, but a proper name referring to <hi type="italic">Gibeah</hi> of Benjamin, the native place of Saul, which was called <hi type="italic">Gibeah of Saul</hi> from the time when Saul resided there as king (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.16">1Sa 10:16</reference> : cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.4">1Sa 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.34">1Sa 15:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.6">2Sa 21:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.29">Isa 10:29</reference>). This is very apparent from the fact that, according to 1Sa 10:10., all the people of Gibeah had known Saul of old, and therefore could not comprehend how he had all at once come to be among the prophets. The name <hi type="italic">Gibeah of God</hi> is here given to the town on account of a <hi type="italic">bamah</hi> or sacrificial height which rose within or near the town (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.13">1Sa 10:13</reference>), and which may possibly have been renowned above other such heights, as the seat of a society of prophets. פלשׁתּים נצבי are not bailiffs of the Philistines, still less columns erected as signs of their supremacy (Thenius), but military posts of the Philistines, as <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.3-1Sam.13.4">1Sa 13:3-4</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.6">2Sa 8:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.14">2Sa 8:14</reference>, clearly show. The allusion here to the posts of the Philistines at Gibeah is connected with what was about to happen to Saul there. At the place where the Philistines, those severe oppressors of Israel, had set up military posts, the Spirit of God was to come upon Saul, and endow him with the divine power that was required for his regal office. “<hi type="italic">And it shall come to pass, when thou comest to the town there, thou wilt light upon a company of prophets coming down from the high place</hi> (<hi type="italic">bamah</hi>, the sacrificial height), <hi type="italic">before them lyre and tambourin, and flute, and harp, and they prophesying</hi>.” חבל signifies a rope or cord, then a <hi type="italic">band</hi> or <hi type="italic">company</hi> of men. It does not follow that because this band of prophets was coming down from the high place, the high place at Gibeah must have been the seat of a school of the prophets. They might have been upon a pilgrimage to Gibeah. The fact that they were preceded by musicians playing, seems to indicate a festal procession. <hi type="italic">Nebel</hi> and <hi type="italic">Kinnor</hi> are stringed instruments which were used after David’s time in connection with the psalmody of divine worship (<reference osisRef="1Chr.13.8">1Ch 13:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.20">1Ch 15:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.33.2">Psa 33:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.43.4">Psa 43:4</reference>, etc.). The <hi type="italic">nebel</hi> was an instrument resembling a <hi type="italic">lyre</hi>, the <hi type="italic">kinnor</hi> was more like a <hi type="italic">guitar</hi> than a harp. <hi type="italic">Toph</hi>: the <hi type="italic">tambourin</hi>, which was played by Miriam at the Red Sea (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.20">Exo 15:20</reference>). <hi type="italic">Chalil</hi>: the <hi type="italic">flute</hi>; see my <hi type="italic">Bibl. Archaeology</hi>, ii. §137. By the prophesying of these prophets we are to understand an ecstatic utterance of religious feelings to the praise of God, as in the case of the seventy elders in the time of Moses (Num 11:25). Whether it took the form of a song or of an enthusiastic discourse, cannot be determined; in any case it was connected with a very energetic action indicative of the highest state of mental excitement. (For further remarks on these societies of prophets, see at 1Sa 19:18.)
entries.94feecf84b651ddda0c8c0fc4b16dac19adbf684: <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.7">1Sa 10:7</reference> <div eID="gen3789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3790" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">When these signs are come unto thee</hi> (the <hi type="italic">Kethibh</hi> תבאינה is to be read תּבאינה, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.45.16">Psa 45:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="Esth.4.4">Est 4:4</reference>; and the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> תּבאנה is a needless emendation), <hi type="italic">do to thee what thy hand findeth</hi>, i.e., act according to the circumstances (for this formula, see Jdg 9:33); <hi type="italic">for God will be with thee</hi>.” The occurrence of the signs mentioned was to assure him of the certainty that God would assist him in all that he undertook as king. The first opportunity for action was afforded him by the Ammonite Nahash, who besieged Jabesh-gilead (<reference osisRef="1Sam.11.1-1Sam.11.15">1Sa 11:1-15</reference>).
entries.5afdfab72e0c1c51fc8fd5fc6a5db52b3aae2be2: <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.8">1Sa 10:8</reference> <div eID="gen3790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3791" type="x-p"/> In conclusion, Samuel gave him an important hint with regard to his future attitude: “<hi type="italic">And goest thou before me down to Gilgal; and, behold, I am coming down to thee, to offer burnt-offerings, and to sacrifice peace-offerings: thou shalt wait seven days, till I come to thee, that I may show thee what thou art to do</hi>.” The infinitive clause וגו להעלות is undoubtedly dependent upon the main clause וירדתּ, and not upon the circumstantial clause which is introduced as a parenthesis. The thought therefore is the following: If Saul went down to Gilgal to offer sacrifice there, he was to wait till Samuel arrived. The construction of the main clause itself, however, is doubtful, since, grammatically considered, ירדתּ can either be a continuation of the imperative עשׂה (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.7">1Sa 10:7</reference>), or can be regarded as independent, and in fact conditional. The latter view, according to which ירדתּ supposes his going down as a possible thing that may take place at a future time, is the one required by the circumstantial clause which follows, and which is introduced by והנּה; for if וירדתּ were intended to be a continuation of the imperative which precedes it, so that Samuel commanded Saul to go down to Gilgal before him, he would have simply announced his coming, that is to say, he would either have said וירדתּי or ארד ואני. The circumstantial clause “and behold I am coming down to thee” evidently presupposes Saul’s going down as a possible occurrence, in the event of which Samuel prescribes the course he is to pursue. But the conditional interpretation of וירדתּ is still more decidedly required by the context. For instance, when Samuel said to Saul that after the occurrence of the three signs he was to do what came to his hand, he could hardly command him immediately afterwards to go to Gilgal, since the performance of what came to his hand might prevent him from going to Gilgal. If, however, Samuel meant that after Saul had finished what came to his hand he was to go down to Gilgal, he would have said, “And after thou hast done this, go down to Gilgal,” etc. But as he does not express himself in this manner, he can only have referred to Saul’s going to Gilgal as an occurrence which, as he foresaw, would take place at some time or other. And to Saul himself this must not only have presented itself as a possible occurrence, but under the existing circumstances as one that was sure to take place; so that the whole thing was not so obscure to him as it is to us, who are only able to form our conclusions from the brief account which lies before us. If we suppose that in the conversation which Samuel had with Saul upon the roof (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.25">1Sa 9:25</reference>), he also spoke about the manner in which the Philistines, who had pushed their outposts as far as Gibeah, could be successfully attacked, he might also have mentioned that Gilgal was the most suitable place for gathering an army together, and for making the necessary preparations for a successful engagement with their foes. If we just glance at the events narrated in the following chapters, for the purpose of getting a clear idea of the thing which Samuel had in view; we find that the three signs announced by Samuel took place on Saul’s return to Gibeah (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.9-1Sam.10.16">1Sa 10:9-16</reference>). Samuel then summoned the people to Mizpeh, where Saul was elected king by lot (<reference osisRef="1Sam.10.17-1Sam.10.27">1Sa 10:17-27</reference>); but Saul returned to Gibeah to his own house even after this solemn election, and was engaged in ploughing the field, when messengers came from Jabesh with the account of the siege of that town by the Ammonites. On receiving this intelligence the Spirit of Jehovah came upon him, so that he summoned the whole nation with energy and without delay to come to battle, and proceeded to Jabesh with the assembled army, and smote the Ammonites (<reference osisRef="1Sam.11.1-1Sam.11.11">1Sa 11:1-11</reference>). Thereupon Samuel summoned the people to come to Gilgal and renew the monarchy there (<reference osisRef="1Sam.11.12-1Sam.11.15">1Sa 11:12-15</reference>); and at the same time he renewed his office of supreme judge (1 Samuel 12), so that now for the first time Saul actually commenced his reign, and began the war against the Philistines (<reference osisRef="1Sam.13.1">1Sa 13:1</reference>), in which, as soon as the latter advanced to Michmash with a powerful army after Jonathan’s victorious engagement, he summoned the people to Gilgal to battle, and after waiting there seven days for Samuel in vain, had the sacrifices offered, on which account as soon as Samuel arrived he announced to him that his rule would not last (1Sa 13:13.). <div eID="gen3791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3792" type="x-p"/> Now, it cannot have been the first of these two gatherings at Gilgal that Samuel had in his mind, but must have been the second. The first is precluded by the simple fact that Samuel summoned the people to go to Gilgal for the purpose of renewing the monarchy; and therefore, as the words “come and let us go to Gilgal” (<reference osisRef="1Sam.11.14">1Sa 11:14</reference>) unquestionably imply, he must have gone thither himself along with the people and the king, so that Saul was never in a position to have to wait for Samuel’s arrival. The second occurrence at Gilgal, on the other hand, is clearly indicated in the words of <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.8">1Sa 13:8</reference>, “<hi type="italic">Saul tarried seven days, according to the set time that Samuel had appointed</hi>,” in which there is almost an express allusion to the instructions given to Saul in the verse before us. But whilst we cannot but regard this as the only true explanation, we cannot agree with Seb. Schmidt, who looks upon the instructions given to Saul in this verse as “a rule to be observed throughout the whole of Samuel’s life,” that is to say, who interprets ירדתּ in the sense of “as often as thou goest down to Gilgal.” For this view cannot be grammatically sustained, although it is founded upon the correct idea, that Samuel’s instructions cannot have been intended as a solitary and arbitrary command, by which Saul was to be kept in a condition of dependence. According to our explanation, however, this is not the case; but there was an inward necessity for them, so far as the government of Saul was concerned. Placed as he was by Jehovah as king over His people, for the purpose of rescuing them out of the power of those who were at that time its most dangerous foes, Saul was not at liberty to enter upon the war against these foes simply by his own will, but was directed to wait till Samuel, the accredited prophet of Jehovah, had completed the consecration through the offering of a solemn sacrifice, and had communicated to him the requisite instructions from God, even though he should have to wait for seven days.<note placement="foot">The difficulty in question has been solved on the whole quite correctly by Brentius. “It is not to be supposed,” he says, “that Samuel was directing Saul to go at once to Gilgal as soon as he should go away from him, and wait there for seven days; but that he was to do this after he had been chosen king by public lot, and having conquered the Ammonites and been confirmed in the kingdom, was about to prepare to make war upon the Philistines, on whose account chiefly it was that he had been called to the kingdom. For the Lord had already spoken thus to Samuel concerning Saul: 'He will save my people from the hands of the Philistines, because I have looked upon my people.' This is the meaning therefore of Samuel’s command: Thou hast been called to the kingdom chiefly for this purpose, that thou mayest deliver Israel from the tyranny of the Philistines. When therefore thou shalt enter upon this work, go down into Gilgal and wait there seven days, until I shall come to thee: for thou shalt then offer a holocaust, though not before I come to thee, and I will show thee what must be done in order that our enemies the Philistines may be conquered. The account of this is given below in 1 Samuel 13, where we learn that Saul violated this command.”</note>
entries.b0c5c9c954182fbf2d0b6cb2f096dce2b635f072: <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.9">1Sa 10:9</reference> <div eID="gen3792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3793" type="x-p"/> When Saul went away from Samuel, to return to Gibeah, “<hi type="italic">God changed to him another heart</hi>,” - a pregnant expression for “God changed him, and gave him another heart” (see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.6">1Sa 10:6</reference>); and all these signs (the signs mentioned by Samuel) happened on that very day. As he left Samuel early in the morning, Saul could easily reach Gibeah in one day, even if the town where he had met with Samuel was situated to the south-west of Rachel’s tomb, as the distance from that tomb to Gibeah was not more than three and a half or four hours.
entries.d7e27411cf3dff9761fec20f4ce9bc7ab815324c: <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.10">1Sa 10:10</reference> <div eID="gen3793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3794" type="x-p"/> The third sign is the only one which is minutely described, because this caused a great sensation at Gibeah, Saul’s home. “<hi type="italic">And they</hi> (Saul and his attendant) <hi type="italic">came thither to Gibeah</hi>.” “<hi type="italic">Thither</hi>” points back to “thither to the city” in <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.5">1Sa 10:5</reference>, and is defined by the further expression “to Gibeah” (Eng. version, “to the hill:” Tr.). The rendering ἔκειθεν (lxx) does not warrant us in changing שׁם into משּׁם; for the latter would be quite superfluous, as it was self-evident that they came to Gibeah from the place where they had been in the company of Samuel.
entries.4c6ee840a43326057726d3126c578b8da41e484d: <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.11">1Sa 10:11</reference> <div eID="gen3794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3795" type="x-p"/> When those who had known Saul of old saw that he prophesied with the prophets, the people said one to another, “<hi type="italic">What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?</hi>” This expression presupposes that Saul’s previous life was altogether different from that of the disciples of the prophets.
entries.e2b747e6bf413e9a3a9adaf0f5c1227270b60dfc: <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.12">1Sa 10:12</reference> <div eID="gen3795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3796" type="x-p"/> And one from thence (i.e., from Gibeah, or from the crowd that was gathered round the prophets) answered, “<hi type="italic">And who is their father?</hi>” i.e., not “who is their president?” which would be a very gratuitous question; but, “is <hi type="italic">their</hi> father a prophet then?” i.e., according to the explanation given by Oehler (Herzog’s <hi type="italic">Real. Enc</hi>. xii. p. 216), “have they the prophetic spirit by virtue of their birth?” Understood in this way, the retort forms a very appropriate “answer” to the expression of surprise and the inquiry, how it came to pass that Saul was among the prophets. If those prophets had not obtained the gift of prophecy by inheritance, but as a free gift of the Lord, it was equally possible for the Lord to communicate the same gift to Saul. On the other hand, the alteration of the text from אביהם (their father) into אביהוּ (his father), according to the lxx, <hi type="italic">Vulg.</hi>, Syr., and Arab., which is favoured by <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, Thenius, and others, must be rejected, for the simple reason that the question, Who is his father? in the mouth of one of the inhabitants of Gibeah, to whom Saul’s father was so well known that they called Saul the son of Kish at once, would have no sense whatever. From this the proverb arose, “Is Saul also among the prophets?” - a proverb which was used to express astonishment at the appearance of any man in a sphere of life which had hitherto been altogether strange to him.
entries.3f9a8f269cbb58f6685b99153357231bd3116f01: <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.13-1Sam.10.16">1Sa 10:13-16</reference> <div eID="gen3796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3797" type="x-p"/> When Saul had left off prophesying, and came to Bamah, his uncle asked him and his attendant where they had been; and Saul told him, that as they had not found the asses anywhere, they had gone to Samuel, and had learned from him that the asses were found. But he did not relate the words which had been spoken by Samuel concerning the monarchy, from unambitious humility (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.22">1Sa 10:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.23">1Sa 10:23</reference>) and not because he was afraid of unbelief and envy, as Thenius follows Josephus in supposing. From the expression “he came to Bamah” (Eng. ver. “to the high place”), we must conclude, that not only Saul’s uncle, but his father also, lived in Bamah, as we find Saul immediately afterwards in his own family circle (see 1Sa 10:14.).
entries.5b6a83a2d6071fb5ef2772619798e604bb46acf9: <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.17-1Sam.10.27">1Sa 10:17-27</reference> <div eID="gen3797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3798" type="x-p"/> Saul’s Election by Lot. - After Samuel had secretly anointed Saul king by the command of God, it was his duty to make provision for a recognition of the man whom God had chosen on the part of the people also. To this end he summoned the people to Mizpeh, and there instructed the tribes to choose a king by lot. As the result of the lot was regarded as a divine decision, not only was Saul to be accredited by this act in the sight of the whole nation as the king appointed by the Lord, but he himself was also to be more fully assured of the certainty of his own election on the part of God. -<note placement="foot">Thenius follows De Wette, and adduces the incompatibility of 1 Samuel 8 and <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.17-1Sam.10.27">1Sa 10:17-27</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1-1Sam.9.10">1Sa 9:1-10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.16">1Sa 9:16</reference>, as a proof that in <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.17-1Sam.10.27">1Sa 10:17-27</reference> we have a different account of the manner in which Saul became king from that given in <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.1-1Sam.9.10">1Sa 9:1-10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.16">1Sa 9:16</reference>, and one which continues the account in 1Sa 8:22. “It is thoroughly inconceivable,” he says, “that Samuel should have first of all anointed Saul king by the instigation of God, and then have caused the lot to be cast, as it were, for the sake of further confirmation; for in that case either the prophet would have tempted God, or he would have made Him chargeable before the nation with an unworthy act of jugglery.” Such an argument as this could only be used by critics who deny not only the inspiration of the prophets, but all influence on the part of the living God upon the free action of men, and cannot therefore render the truth of the biblical history at all doubtful. Even <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi> sees no discrepancy here, and observes in his history (<hi type="italic">Gesch. </hi>iii. p. 32): “If we bear in mind the ordinary use made of the sacred lot at that time, we shall find that there is nothing but the simple truth in the whole course of the narrative. The secret meeting of the seer with Saul was not sufficient to secure a complete and satisfactory recognition of him as king; it was also necessary that the Spirit of Jehovah should single him out publicly in a solemn assembly of the nation, and point him out as the man of Jehovah.”</note>  <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.17">1Sa 10:17</reference> העם is the nation in its heads and representatives. <hi type="italic">Samuel</hi> selected <hi type="italic">Mizpeh</hi> for this purpose, because it was there that he had once before obtained for the people, by prayer, a great victory over the Philistines (1Sa 7:5.).

Or, <ns0:hi>to the House of God,</ns0:hi> i. e. to <ns0:hi>Kiriath<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jearim,</ns0:hi> where the Ark, the habitation of God, now was, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 7. 1, 2, 16.</ns0:note>, one carrying three kids, and another carrying three loaves of bread <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Which might be Offered, either by themselves, as <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 2. 4. or with other Sacrifices.</ns0:note>, and another car<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rying a bottle of wine <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Which was poured forth in Drink-Offerings. See <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 23. 13. <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 15. 5.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                     </ns0:note> salute thee, and give thee two <ns0:hi>loaves</ns0:hi> of bread <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Two of those three designed for Sacrifice, supposing they could easily procure a supply of other Loaves at <ns0:hi>Bethel.</ns0:hi> But the more strange the Present was, the more fit it was for a sign of Gods extraordinary Providence in <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fairs.</ns0:note>, which thou shalt receive of their hand.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 After that thou shalt come to the hill of God <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">An Hill near <ns0:hi>Geba,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Gibeah</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Benjamin,</ns0:hi> where a Ga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rison of <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> was, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 13. 3. called here <ns0:hi>the Hill of God,</ns0:hi> because it was a place Devoted to the Service of God; either for Sacrifice, this being an <ns0:hi>high place,</ns0:hi> as it here follows; or, for a School or Colledge of Prophets.</ns0:note>, where <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the garison of the Philistines: and it shall come to pass, when thou art come thither to the city <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />joyning to that Hill.</ns0:note>, that thou shalt meet a company of pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phets <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>Prophets</ns0:hi> here, and in such like places, he understands Persons that did wholly Devote them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves to Religious studies and exercises, such as Preaching, Praying, Praising of God, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> For the term of <ns0:hi>Prophesying</ns0:hi> is not onely given to the most Eminent act of it, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> foretelling things to come; but also to Preaching, as <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12. 6. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 14. 31, 32. 1 <ns0:hi>Thess.</ns0:hi> 5. 20. and to the making or Sing<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of Psalms, or Songs of Praise to God, as 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 25. 1, 2, 3. And they that wholly attended upon these things, are oft called <ns0:hi>Sons of the Prophets,</ns0:hi> which were com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monly combined into Companies or Colledges, as 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 2. 3, 5. that they might more conveniently edify and assist one another in Gods work. Which Institution God was pleased so far to Honour and Bless, that sometimes he Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />municated unto those Persons the knowledge of future things, as 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 2. 3, 5.</ns0:note> coming down from the high place <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Where, either, their habitation was, or they had now been offering Sacrifice. And although they used to perform this following exercise, either in their Colledge, or in the place of their Sacrifices; yet now they did it in the descent of the Hill, which probably was beside their Custome, and therefore more proper for a sign to <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> of a more than ordinary hand of God towards him.</ns0:note>, with a psaltery, and a tabret, and a pipe, and a harp before them <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Such Instruments of Musick being then used by Prophets and other persons, for the exhileration and excitation of their spirits in Gods Service. See 2 King. 3. 15.</ns0:note>, and they shall prophesie <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Either sing Gods Prai<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ses, or speak of the things of God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:224" />6 And the Spirit of the LORD will come upon thee <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>will leap</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>rush upon thee,</ns0:hi> to wit, for a season. So it may be opposed to the <ns0:hi>Spirits resting</ns0:hi> upon a man, as <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 11. 25. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 11. 2.</ns0:note>, and thou shalt prophesie with them, and shalt be turned into another man <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Thou shalt be suddenly endowed and acted with another Spirit, filled with skill of Divine things, with Courage, and Wisdome, and Magnanimi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty; and other qualifications befitting thy Dignity.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> it shall come to pass that when these signs, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> let it be when these signs <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Which were certain evidences of Gods calling of him to the Kingdom, because they were all future contingencies, which none but God could infallibly know or foretel.</ns0:note> are come unto thee, <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> do for thee as thy hand shall find</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> thou do as occasion shall serve thee <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>do what thy hand findeth to do; i. e.</ns0:hi> As thou shalt have a Call and opportunity. He doth not intend that he should take the Kingly Government upon him, before his Call to it was known to, and owned by the People, which had been pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posterous and dangerous; but that he should dispose his mind to a readiness of undertaking any Publick Service when necessity required it, and he should be called to his Office.</ns0:note>, for God <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> with thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And thou shalt go down before me to Gilgal, and behold, I will come down unto thee, to offer burnt-offerings, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> to sacrifice sacrifices of peace<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />offerings: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 13. 8.</ns0:note> seven days shalt thou tarry till I come to thee <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">This, though now mentioned and commanded, yet was not immediately to be performed; as is evident, partly from the whole course of the Story, which shews, That <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Samuel,</ns0:hi> and the People, first met at <ns0:hi>Mizpeh,</ns0:hi> v. 17, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> where <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> was chosen by God, and accepted by the Peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple as King; and afterwards went to <ns0:hi>Gilgal</ns0:hi> once before the time here spoken of, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 11. 14, 15. and partly, by com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />paring this place with <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 13. 8, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> where we find <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> charged with the violation of this Command, two years af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter the giving of it, as appears from <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 13. 1, 2. <ns0:hi>Qu.</ns0:hi> How then is this to be understood? <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> 1. This may be given as a standing Rule for <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> to observe while <ns0:hi>Samuel</ns0:hi> and he lived; That in case of any great future difficulties, as the Invasion of Enemies, <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> should resort to <ns0:hi>Gilgal,</ns0:hi> and call the people thither, and tarry there Seven days, which was but a reasonable and necessary time for the gathering of the People, and for the coming of <ns0:hi>Samuel</ns0:hi> thither. For though this be related as but once done, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 13. yet <ns0:hi>Iosephus</ns0:hi> affirms, that it was to be constantly practised upon all such occasions. And <ns0:hi>Gilgal</ns0:hi> was chosen for this purpose as a very fit place; partly, because that place was famous for the solemn renewing of the Covenant between God and Israel, <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 4. and for other eminent instances of Gods favour to them, the remembrance whereof was a notable confirma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion of their Faith; and partly, because it was a very con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venient place for the Tribes within and without <ns0:hi>Iordan</ns0:hi> to assemble, and consult, and unite their Forces together upon such occasions. If you ask, Why then <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> did not practise this Precept upon the first Invasion of the <ns0:hi>Ammonites?</ns0:hi> It may be answered, That this was a Rule for <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> when he and <ns0:hi>Samuel</ns0:hi> were asunder, whereas they were together in that expedition, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 11. 7. And further, That necessity did excuse the Violation of this Precept then, because <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> could not wait for <ns0:hi>Samuel,</ns0:hi> nor forbear his action for Seven days, as is evident from <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 11. 3, 9, 10. Or, 2. (which I propose with submission to the Learned and Judicious) This may be here added as another sign to confirm his Faith, which having strengthned by three foregoing signs, he now fortifies it by another sign which was to follow afterwards; it being very usual for God to give men signs to confirm their Faith from future Events; as <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 3. 12. 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 19. 29. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 7. 13, 14. So the meaning may be this; Another sign I will add to strengthen thy Faith; <ns0:hi>Thou shalt</ns0:hi> in due time, and upon a great occasion which shall then happen, <ns0:hi>go down before me to Gilgal, and</ns0:hi> there <ns0:hi>I will come down unto thee to offer—Sacrifices, &c.</ns0:hi> But when thou comest thither, be sure <ns0:hi>thou tarry there seven days,</ns0:hi> and then <ns0:hi>I will come,</ns0:hi> as I have said, and give thee necessary Instructions and Assistance, as the matter shall re<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e.</ns0:note>, and shew thee what thou shalt do.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And when they came thither to the hill, behold, a company of prophets met him, and the Spirit of God came upon him, and he prophesied among them <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The accomplishment of the two former signs is sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posed, and this onely of the third is expressed, because this was more eminent and publick than the former; the other were onely Transient acts, which passed in private between two or three persons meeting together, and passing by one another; but this was a more permanent and more notorious sign, done in a more solemn manner, and before many, and very considerable witnesses.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And it came to pass, when all that knew him before-time, saw, that behold, he prophesied among the prophets, then the people said <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> a man to his neigh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bour.</ns0:note> one to ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, What <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> this <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> is come unto the son of Kish <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">What means this strange and prodigions event?</ns0:note>

                        </ns0:gap>p. 19. 24.</ns0:note> is Saul <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">A man never instructed, nor exercised in, nor enclined to these matters; a man ever thought fitter to look to his fathers As<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ses, than to bear a part in the sacred exercises of the Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phets.</ns0:note> also among the prophets?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And one <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> from thence.</ns0:note> of the same place <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>one from thence, i. e.</ns0:hi> One of the company there present, or one of the Prophets there prophecying.</ns0:note> answered, and said, But who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> their father <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Who is the Father of all these Prophets of whom you speak, and among whom <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> now is one? Who is it that instructs and inspires them with this holy Art, but God? They have it not from their Natural Parents, nor from their Civil Education, but by Inspiration from God, who, when he pleaseth, can inspire <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> or any other man with the same skill. And therefore wonder not at this matter, but give God the glory of it. <ns0:hi>Father</ns0:hi> is here put for Teacher, or Instructor, as it is used; as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 4. 20, 21. <ns0:hi>Matt.</ns0:hi> 23. 9. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 4. 15. And hence the Scholars are called <ns0:hi>sons of the Prophets.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>? Therefore it became a proverb <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Used when any strange, unlikely, or unexpected thing happened.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>Is</ns0:hi> Saul also among the pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phets?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And when he had made an end of prophe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sying, he came to the high place <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Returning thither with the Prophets, there to pra<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> God for these wonderful favours, and to beg counsel and help from God in this high business.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 ¶ And Sauls uncle <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Being there present, and observing this great alteration in his Nephew.</ns0:note> said unto him, and to his servant, Whither went ye? and he said, To seek the asses: and when we saw that <ns0:hi>they were</ns0:hi> no where, we came to Samuel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And Sauls uncle said, Tell me, I pray thee, what Samuel said unto you.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And Saul said unto his uncle, He told us plainly that the asses were found. But of the matter of the kingdom, whereof Samuel spake, he told him not <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Partly in obedience to <ns0:hi>Samuel,</ns0:hi> who obliged him to secre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy: partly, from an humble modesty which appeared in him, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 22. and partly, in prudence, lest by an unseasonable pub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lishing of it, he should raise envy in some, disbelief and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tempt in others, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause the Ark was carried thither upon this occasion. Or, 2. Because God is present in all the Assemblies of his Peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, whereof this was an eminent one, See 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 19. 6<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 82. 1. Or, 3. Because they did in a manner E<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                        </ns0:gap>ect a Tribunal for God; and intreated, and consequently ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tained his Presence there to supervise and direct the whole business by his sentence, which also he did, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 19, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> See of this Phrase <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 11. 11. and 20. 1.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>to</ns0:hi> Mizpeh <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">A City of <ns0:hi>Benja<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />min, Ios.</ns0:hi> 13. 26. where all Israel had met before upon a Publick and solemn occasion, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 7. 5.</ns0:note>,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:225" />18 And said unto the children of Israel, Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, I brought up Israel out of Egypt, and delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians, and out of the hand of all king<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />doms <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">To wit, the neighbouring Kingdoms, which molested you from time to time.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> of them that oppressed you.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And ye have this day rejected your God <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">You this day declare, That you persist in your former act of rejecting Gods Government, See on <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 8. 7.</ns0:note>, who himself saved you <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Who by his own special Providence took care to raise up Judges and Saviours for you, and to deliver you at all times, when you needed his help, and did not by your Sins obstruct it.</ns0:note> out of all your adversi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties, and your tribulations: and ye have said un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to him <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Unto me his Prophet and Ambassador; and conse<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quently unto the Lord whom I represented, and in whose Name I spake and acted.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>Nay,</ns0:hi> but set a king over us. Now there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore present your selves before the LORD by your tribes, and by your thousands <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">For each Tribe was divided into thousands, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 10. 36. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 33. 17. <ns0:hi>Iosh.</ns0:hi> 22. 14, 21. <ns0:hi>Mic.</ns0:hi> 5. 2. as in <ns0:hi>England,</ns0:hi> Counties are into Hundreds.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20. And when Samuel had caused all the tribes of Israel to come near <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Unto the place appointed for the casting of Lots.</ns0:note>, the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Josh. 7. 14, 16.</ns0:note> tribe of Benjamin was taken <ns0:note n="*" place="bottom">Which Tribe was now preferred before <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> because the Kingdom was freely promised by God to <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> and was to be given to him in love; but now the Kingdom was in a manner forced from God, and given to them in anger, <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 13. 11. and therefore conferred upon an obscure Tribe.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 When he had caused the tribe of Benja<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />min to come near by their families, the family of Matri was taken, and Saul the son of Kish was ta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken: and when they sought him, he could not be found.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 Therefore they enquired of the LORD <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Either by <ns0:hi>Urim</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Thummim,</ns0:hi> which was the usual way of enquiry, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 27. 21. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 23. 9. and 28 6. Or by <ns0:hi>Samuel,</ns0:hi> who by his Prayer procured an answer.</ns0:note> further, if the man should yet come thither: and the LORD answered, Behold, he hath hid him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self among the stuff <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Among the Carriages or Baggage of the People there Assembled. This he might do, because he either had, or at least would be thought to have a modest sence of his own unworthiness, which was a likely way to commend him to the People.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 And they ran and fetched him thence, and when he stood among the people, he was higher than any of the people, from his shoulders and upward.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 And Samuel said to all the people, See ye him whom the Lord hath chosen, that <ns0:hi>there</ns0:hi> is none like him among all the people <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">As to the height of his Bodily Stature, which was in it self commendable in a King, and some kind of indication of great endowments of Mind.</ns0:note>? and all the peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple shouted, and said, <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> Let the King live.</ns0:note> God save the king <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>Let the king live;</ns0:hi> to wit, long and prosperously; for an Afflicted Life is repu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted a kind of Death, and is oft so called. Hereby they accept and own him for their King, and promise Subjection to him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 Then Samuel told the people the manner of the kingdom <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Not <ns0:hi>the manner of the King,</ns0:hi> of which he had spoken before, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 8. 11, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>of the Kingdom;</ns0:hi> to wit, the Laws and Rules by which the Kingly Government was to be managed; agreeable to those mentioned <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 17. 16, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> which peradventure <ns0:hi>Samuel</ns0:hi> did expound, and apply to their particular case.</ns0:note>, and wrote <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> in a book, and laid it up before the LORD <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Before the Ark, or in the Sanctuary, where it was kept safe from depravation.</ns0:note>, and Samuel sent all the peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple away, every man to his house.</ns0:p>
